architecture.mechanism: Thermal degradation of polymer-based materials through controlled pyrolysis at elevated temperatures (350–550 °C) to convert waste plastics into defined solid, oil, and gas products, enabling targeted thermal conversion of hydrocarbon-bearing components.
architecture.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal-degradation/pyrolysis step to the failed transmission oil cooler's polymer (plastic) end-tank or internal turbulence-baffle components recovered from warranty units, to characterize and verify the thermal stability envelope of those polymers against the cooler-internal operating temperatures reached during the documented 2020 Ford Explorer highway-tow/duty-cycle failure (mileage 1,896, in-motion breakdown), and use the pyrolysis temperature profiles (350–550 °C) as a screening reference to set an upper-bound thermal limit for replacement polymer selection in the cooler packaging.
architecture.expected_effect: Identification of the polymer decomposition onset temperature of the installed cooler components, allowing selection or reformulation of an end-tank/baffle polymer whose thermal degradation threshold exceeds the peak bulk-oil/interface temperatures reached in the 2020 Explorer transmission cooler under highway load, thereby reducing in-service thermal-degradation-driven cooler cracking, internal leakage, and subsequent transmission failure.
architecture.falsification_test: Subject representative samples of the cooler end-tank/baffle polymer (new and field-returned from the Explorer failure) to TGA/DSC and bench pyrolysis at the referenced 350–550 °C setpoints using the face-mask study's method; if the installed polymer shows no measurable mass loss or property change at or below the measured cooler peak skin/internal temperature (e.g., ≤ 200 °C) and shows decomposition only above that temperature, the thermal-degradation mechanism is falsified for this failure mode and root cause must be re-evaluated (e.g., coolant-side corrosion, vibration fatigue, or seal failure).
